extracted.intended_audience: readers of colonial-era ethnography, anthropologists, and general readers interested in West African customs
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive ethnographic account of West African beliefs and customs (witchcraft, funerary rites, secret societies, apparitions, initiation practices) drawn from colonial-era field observation. Focuses on practices, local explanations, and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witch behaviour and countermeasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Local belief that witches walk naked along the beach at night, eat sea crabs, emit a bright light, and can be made to blaze until morning if a certain medicine is thrown over them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: throw the medicine over the witch so it 'remain[s] blazing until morning time, running to and fro...and when the dawn comes the fire burns the witch right up.' No explicit ritual formula given beyond this description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surf purification for postpartum women and widows (eight-day rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coastal Tschwi custom of bringing women who have had children and widows to the surf after a period of eight days from birth or death for purification ceremonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widows remain in the house for eight days neglecting their person, then relatives come with musical instruments and mint (burned) to sing to the Srah, strip the widow, throw her rags into the surf, clothe her in dark blue baft brought for the occasion, and hold a festival; remarriage before this ceremony is believed to bring the dead husband's Srah mischief to any new husband.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inland extended mourning and funerary accompaniments
rubrics_metrics.description: In inland Gold Coast districts, widows mourn for several months, and selected people (slaves and free men) are killed to escort the dead to Srahmandazi; goods (gold dust, velvets, silks, satins) are thrown into the grave to provide merchandise for the deceased in the under-world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice contrasts with coast quick burials; among some Bantu (Cameroon) velvets etc. are buried with the dead — possibly for glorification of living relatives (display of wealth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soul-span doctrine and Sisa concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that each human soul has a definite earthly existence (e.g., thirty years). If the body is killed before the allotted span, the leftover years are spent as a restless spirit (Sisa) causing sickness, mischief, and trouble for survivors until properly guided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prematurely-dislodged soul will knock about old haunts, cause damage, pull off roofs, and affect surviving husbands of wives, until funeral 'custom' or spells teach the soul the path to Srahmandazi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funeral 'custom' (ritual) required to guide souls to Srahmandazi
rubrics_metrics.description: The funeral 'custom' or rites performed by relatives and priests instruct the soul in the path to Srahmandazi; without it a soul may remain as a nuisance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rituals and incantations can enable an incomplete-life soul to enter a newborn or to learn the way down the dark path; priests charge a fee but performing the work prevents further trouble from the dead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Srahmandazi cosmology and post-mortem society
rubrics_metrics.description: Srahmandazi (the underworld) is pictured as like this world — towns, markets, rivers; suns set there when rising here; inhabitants may remain at the age they left or grow to a prime of life; its inhabitants continue palavers and disputes which may affect the living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there are outbreaks of sickness on earth it may be interpreted as a palaver below; priests collect earthly testimony and transmit evidence to the court in Srahmandazi to avoid living journeys below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparitions of gods and differential effects on priests vs laity
rubrics_metrics.description: Gods (e.g., Sasabonsum, Tando) regularly appear to their priests and occasionally to laity; appearances are harmless or beneficial to priests but often harmful to laypeople.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tando (the Hater) is malicious and may appear as a crying male child to be taken in, then cause contagious disease—illustrating gods' hostile tactics; driver ants may be considered messengers and are not to be molested in Tando's territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-human/thing apparitions and local taboos
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only human spirits but objects (spears, pitchers) may have ghosts that act harmfully or trick people — e.g., pitcher ready filled that crumbles to dust when taken from a haunted spring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples emphasize local caution about taking unaccountable objects at evening or from springs; consequences include loss of property and danger to life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blood-omen ('blood come before') belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearance of blood in a house (blood 'coming before') is interpreted as an uncanny omen indicating a forthcoming death or unusual fate, because blood represents life and its unexplained presence is mysterious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by a household where blood repeatedly appeared and later a relative died by a bloodless accident (broken neck), interpreted as the blood 'having to go somewhere.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitudes to shedding blood in judicial execution
rubrics_metrics.description: There is aversion to certain kinds of blood-shedding in judicial executions, illustrated by a chief who ordered repeated drownings and then execution and was believed to die by spitting blood before the year was out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author conjectures an underlying taboo or idea affecting execution methods (e.g., tying thieves to stakes, driver-ant executions), but notes investigation is difficult due to language and social barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret societies as chiefly judicial institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tribe has secret societies (e.g., Poorah, Oru, Egbo, Isyogo, Ukuku, Ikun, Lukuku); they are not essentially religious but mainly judicial, with rituals and a presiding spirit distinct from a god in European sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rituals vary in detail but share broad common lines; societies often keep women 'in order' and maintain social discipline through their rites and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender segregation and prohibition of cross-sex participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Male and female secret societies are generally rigidly kept apart; women are usually forbidden to participate in male rites or learn their secrets, and men likewise are punished for infringing female mysteries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations can be met with death; the prohibition underlies social control and the societies' ability to regulate behaviour of the opposite sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiation age and general initiation structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Young free people are usually admitted to societies at about eight to ten years of age: boys to male societies, girls to female; initiation involves seclusion and instruction in secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initiation often includes renaming, adoption of a secret language, seclusion in forest groves or huts, and a formal period of separation from prior life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boys' initiation regimen
rubrics_metrics.description: Boys are tattooed when practised, handed to instructors, live with other initiates (often in the forest) for a year, naked and smeared with clay, trained to endure hardship, sometimes taught raiding and warfare, and take a new name and secret language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On return they are ceremonially welcomed and pretend to have forgotten their former life; in some tribes boys remain under elders' rule until they have killed a man (Yoruba example) as demonstration of courage and acquisition of a soul-slave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Girls' initiation and fattening-house customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Girls' initiation can involve seclusion in huts or magic woods; in Grain Coast/Calabar the 'fattening-house' is used to fatten girls pre-marriage, with white clay applied while in seclusion and when temporarily leaving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: White clay serves an initiatory or protective function (local explanations vary — some say to prevent perspiration and assist fattening); girls may be kept covered and fed fat-producing foods like fou-fou with palm oil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in duration of seclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of seclusion varies by area: San Salvador boys six months, Cameroon boys twelve months; girls' seclusion time varies with circumstances; initiation schedules are tribe-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duration is a tribal prescription and linked to the completeness of instruction and the society's norms for readiness to re-enter community life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret societies' judicial roles and methods of discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies exercise jurisdiction over many crimes (Egbo exercises jurisdiction over all classes except witchcraft) and maintain discipline through rites—masked processions, whips, cutlasses, placing paraphernalia to enforce social compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods may seem odd to Europeans (rushing about in disguise, lashing passersby), but are effective means of maintaining order in local context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egbo society: graded ranks, fees, and leverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Egbo has many grades of initiation, is well-developed, and rising ranks require large fees (reported 1,000–1,500 pounds English). High-rank members can mobilize their grade as enforcement against debtors of lower grades; higher grades outrank lower ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Becoming influential in tribe often requires buying into high Egbo grades; the society can place Egbo paraphernalia at a man's doorway preventing him leaving until it is removed—practical leverage used to enforce payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egbo spirit-ark capture and public manifestations
rubrics_metrics.description: Egbo spirit is captured in a box/ark in the bush, carried into town with drumming and dancing; the ark may emit a strange, non-human voice and pronouncements (the ark as locus of authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture and public display produce town-wide celebrations and temporary legal or moral pronouncements; outsiders may suspect a person concealed in the ark but the ritual voice is treated as the spirit's authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practices of secrecy, theatricality and social control (Ikun example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Societies use staged manifestations and theatrical devices to enforce belief and stamp out skepticism (e.g., men staged an Ikun apparition by concealing a man under the hut-floor to frighten skeptical women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This demonstrates deliberate deployment of ritual theatre to maintain social cohesion and re-establish reverence; secrecy and staged fear can be used to detect or punish skeptics and to extort payments for 'immunity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tattooing, painting, and cicatrices as bodily markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Skin decoration appears as paint or cicatrices; paint patterns may be followed by a wash that makes the unpainted skin rise between the painted pattern; cicatrices are produced by cutting and inserting the silk-cotton fluff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tattooing is comparatively rare and not used for decoration alone; cicatrices can be tribal marks or decorative; patterns and methods vary by region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between general tribal secret societies and 'leopard'/murder societies
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret societies (youth-initiating, judicial) are generally distinct from leopard or murder societies; the latter are clandestine murder societies whose practices usually include cannibalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some individuals may belong to multiple societies; evidence of distinction is stronger among Negro groups than Bantu in the author's sample, but local variation exists.
